description:
A **region** is a contiguous byte range, however it was obtained: an ordinary
allocation, or a file mapped `MAP_SHARED` that another process can map by
name. A `BumpAllocator` carves one up.

The rule that makes it a library rather than a helper is that `claim` returns
an **offset**, not an address. A shared mapping lands somewhere different in
every process that maps it, so anything built inside a region has to refer to
itself by offset; a reader adds its own `base()` and it all resolves. What
that buys is a structure you can hand to someone else — through a file, a
shared mapping, an object store — without serialising it.

    var bump = BumpAllocator[MappedRegion](MappedRegion("/tmp/batch", size))
    var header = bump.claim(8)
    var payload = bump.append(some_bytes)
    bump.unsafe_ptr(header).unsafe_bitcast[Int64]()[unsafe_offset=0] = Int64(payload)
    bump^.close()          # unmaps; the file stays

and on the other side:

    var mapped = SharedMapping("/tmp/batch")   # read-only, unmapped at end of scope
    var head = mapped.span[DType.int64](header, 1)[0]
    var values = mapped.span[DType.uint8](Int(head), n)

## Dropping is safe, giving away is explicit

A region frees or unmaps itself at end of scope, because a leaked mapping has
no other symptom. `into_raw()` is how an export says the bytes are the
consumer's now: it consumes the region so the destructor does not run.

## What it does not do

**Grow.** A fixed range, so `claim` raises rather than reallocating. Size it
up front: a producer that knows its total sizes it exactly, one that does not
can over-allocate a mapping, since untouched pages never materialise.

**Free a piece.** The whole region goes at once.

**Describe itself.** A reader needs a manifest, and what that looks like
belongs to whoever owns the payload.

modules.summary: A cursor that only moves forward.
modules.description:
`BumpAllocator` holds one number — how far into the region it has got — and
allocating is "give me where the cursor is, then move it on by `n`". No free
list, no search, no per-allocation header: two instructions. The price is that
an individual piece can never be freed, which is the usual arena trade and
suits data that is born together and dies together.

## Offsets, not addresses

`claim` returns an **offset from the start of the region**, and anything
stored inside a region refers to the rest of it by offset. A shared mapping
lands at a different address in every process that maps it, so an address
written into it means something only to the process that wrote it; a reader
adds its own `base()` and everything resolves.

`span` is how to read and write what has been claimed: a typed view that
borrows the allocator, so the compiler knows when it stops being valid.
`unsafe_address` is the way back to a raw address, for the moment one has to
be written into a C structure whose consumer is this process.

structs.name: BumpAllocator
structs.summary: Hands out 8-byte-aligned offsets into a region, front to back.
structs.description:
Arrow wants every buffer 8-byte aligned — consumers cast them in place —
so alignment is the allocator's job rather than each caller's.

fields.name: used
fields.summary: How far the cursor has moved: the region's occupied prefix.

overloads.signature: def claim(mut self, n: Int) -> Int
overloads.summary: Reserve `n` bytes and return their **offset** from the base.
overloads.description:
Raises rather than growing: a region is a fixed range, and nothing
that has already handed out an offset could survive being moved.

overloads.signature: def append[dtype: DType, //](mut self, data: Span[Scalar[dtype]]) -> Int
overloads.summary: Claim room for `data`, copy it in, and return where it went.
overloads.description:
Any scalar element type, so a buffer of `Int32` offsets goes in as
itself rather than as an address and a byte count.

overloads.signature: def span[dtype: DType](ref self, offset: Int, count: Int) -> Span[Scalar[dtype], origin_of(self)]
overloads.summary: `count` values of `dtype` at `offset`, as a view of this allocator.
overloads.description:
The view borrows the allocator: writable when the allocator is
reached through `mut`, read-only otherwise, and unusable once it is
closed, moved or dropped — all checked by the compiler. Claiming more
while a view is alive is fine, because `claim` never moves anything.

The offset is one this allocator handed out, so a bad one is a bug
rather than bad input: it is a `debug_assert` against what has been
claimed, not a raise.

overloads.signature: def unsafe_ptr(self, offset: Int) -> Pointer[UInt8, MutUntrackedOrigin]
overloads.summary: A writable pointer to `offset`, valid in this process only.
`offset` as an address in this process.
overloads.description:
The only place an address belongs: writing one into a C structure
whose consumer is this process. Anything a peer will read stores the
offset instead.

overloads.summary: Give the region back now; it would go at end of scope anyway.
Give up ownership of the region; returns its base address.
overloads.description:
What an export does when the bytes become the consumer's — the Arrow
C Data Interface release callback frees them later.

modules.summary: POSIX, for the two backings that need it.
modules.description:
Kept apart from the regions themselves so that a reader of `region.mojo` sees
what a region *is* rather than which integer `O_CREAT` happens to be on this
platform.

overloads.summary: `O_CREAT`, which is not the same number on both platforms.
overloads.description:
macOS has 0x0200 and Linux 0x40. Getting it wrong does not fail loudly —
it opens with some other flag set — so it is spelled out here rather than
inherited from a header nobody reads.

overloads.summary: `O_TRUNC`: 0x0400 on macOS, 0x200 on Linux.
A NUL-terminated copy, owned by the caller across the FFI call.

overloads.signature: def open_file(path: String, flags: Int, mode: Int = Int(384)) -> Int
overloads.summary: `open(2)`, as an fd.
overloads.description:
`open` is variadic in C — `int open(const char *, int, ...)` — and a
variadic call has a different ABI from a fixed one on arm64, so the
fixed-argument count has to be declared or the mode lands in the wrong
place. It fails at LLVM lowering rather than at the call, so the error
does not point here.

overloads.summary: The size of the file at `path`, from the standard library's `stat`.
overloads.description:
This used to be `lseek(fd, 0, SEEK_END)` through `external_call`. The
standard library declares `lseek` too, for `FileHandle.seek`, with
different argument types, and one program can't hold two declarations of
one C function: any binary that used both failed to compile with
"existing function with conflicting signature".

overloads.signature: def truncate(fd: Int, size: Int) -> Bool
def map_file(fd: Int, size: Int, writable: Bool) -> Int
overloads.summary: `mmap(..., MAP_SHARED)`; 0 when the kernel refused.

modules.summary: Where a region's bytes come from, and what giving them back means.
modules.description:
A region is a contiguous byte range. What differs between one and the next is
how it was obtained — an allocation, a mapped file, later perhaps a slab in an
object store or a pinned buffer on the way to a GPU — and what releasing it
means. Nothing that carves a region up needs to know which it has.

## Dropping one is safe; giving it away is explicit

A region frees or unmaps itself when it goes out of scope, because the failure
it would otherwise have is invisible: a leaked mapping produces no error, no
crash and nothing in the output, and the file stays open through it.

`into_raw` is the way out for the case that is not a leak — an export whose
bytes become the consumer's, freed later by its own release callback. It
consumes the region, so the destructor does not also run, and the transfer is
readable at the call site instead of being implied by an omission.

Mojo can do better than this: `@explicit_destroy` with a `not Deinitable`
conformance makes abandoning a region a *compile* error naming the method to
call. It is not used here because it needs a September-2026 nightly, and these
tins build on `mojo-compiler` 1.2.0. Worth revisiting when stable catches up —
it turns a safe default into an impossible mistake.

structs.name: HeapRegion
structs.summary: An ordinary allocation: what an in-process export has always used.

overloads.summary: Freed when it goes out of scope, unless `into_raw` took it.
Hand the allocation back, now rather than at the end of scope.
Give up ownership; returns the base address.
overloads.description:
For a consumer that will free the bytes itself — the Arrow C Data
Interface being the case this exists for, where the release callback
on the exported array is what eventually frees the block.

structs.name: MappedRegion
structs.summary: A file mapped `MAP_SHARED`, which a peer process can map by name.
structs.description:
The file is the handle. A consumer needs the path and nothing else:
everything inside is laid out by offset, so it can map the same bytes
wherever its own address space happens to put them.

fields.name: path
fields.summary: Where a peer will find these bytes.

overloads.signature: def __init__(out self, var path: String, size: Int)
overloads.summary: Create (or truncate) `path` at `size` bytes and map it writable.
Unmapped when it goes out of scope, unless `into_raw` took it.
Drop this process's view of the bytes. The file stays.
overloads.description:
Unlinking is deliberately not done here: the consumer may not have
mapped it yet, and when the bytes stop being needed is the caller's
business rather than the region's.

overloads.summary: Leave the mapping in place and give up ownership of it.

structs.name: SharedMapping
structs.summary: The consumer's half: a peer's region, mapped read-only by path.
structs.description:
It lands wherever this address space puts it, and everything inside is
reached by offset from there. Unmapped at end of scope, like a region.

Views come out of `span` and `bytes`, and carry this mapping's origin.
That makes two mistakes compile errors rather than crashes: writing
through a view (the pages are `PROT_READ`, so a write would fault), and
holding a view after the mapping has gone (it would point at nothing).

What the types cannot promise is anything about the bytes: offsets come
from another process's manifest, so `span` checks them against the
mapping at run time, and the producer can still rewrite or truncate the
file underneath a view.

It is deliberately not a `Region`: a region is something a
`BumpAllocator` carves up and writes into, and this one cannot be written.

fields.name: path
fields.summary: The file these bytes were mapped from.

overloads.summary: Map `path` read-only, all of it.
Unmapped when it goes out of scope.
How many bytes are mapped: the file's length when it was opened.

overloads.signature: def span[dtype: DType](self, offset: Int, count: Int) -> Span[Scalar[dtype], origin_of(self)]
overloads.summary: `count` values of `dtype` starting `offset` bytes in, read-only.
overloads.description:
Raises if they do not fit inside the mapping, or if `offset` is not
aligned for `dtype` — both things a manifest from another process can
get wrong, and neither of which a type can rule out.

overloads.summary: The whole mapping, as bytes.
Address of byte 0 in this process, untracked.
overloads.description:
For handing a buffer to something outside Mojo's view — an Arrow
C Data import, a foreign function. The address is only good while
this mapping is alive, and nothing checks that.

traits.name: Region
traits.summary: A contiguous byte range that something else owns the lifetime of.

overloads.summary: Address of byte 0 **in this process**.
How many bytes it holds.
Give the bytes back: free, unmap, whatever this region means.
Give up ownership; returns the base address.
overloads.description:
For bytes that become someone else's — an Arrow export whose release
callback frees them later. Consuming, so the destructor does not also
run.

overloads.summary: Map an existing file read-only; returns `(address, length)`.
overloads.description:
Nothing ever unmaps what this returns. Kept for one release while callers
move to `SharedMapping`.
overloads.deprecated: use SharedMapping(path): it unmaps itself and checks offsets
